title: Algebra A: Algebraic Fractions

findings.finding: Eleven whole tasks recur unchanged without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: The repeated expressions and LCD pairs supply previously completed tasks instead of fresh instances. The multiplication/division comparison in p20-q3 should remain intact when its repeated items change.
findings.checked: Compared every named pair's complete expression, values, givens and task instruction. No diagrams distinguish the copies. The instruction to simplify before multiplying changes the requested approach but does not explicitly ask students to revisit or compare earlier working. The operation contrast within p20-q3 does not state a purpose for copying tasks from p18.
findings.assumptions: Tasks are completed in booklet order; no additional retrieval purpose is supplied.

repair.proposal: Replace the later copies as follows: p5-q1-e: 4y/7 − y/7, answer 3y/7. p6-q2-e: fractions with the existing blank numerators and denominators 4 and 6, LCD 12; p6-q2-f: denominators 6 and 8, LCD 24. p10-q5-r1c2: 5x + x/2, answer 11x/2. p14-q2-a: x/4 × 3/5, answer 3x/20; p14-q2-c: 3/7 × 2a/5, answer 6a/35; p14-q4-a: 8x/7 × 5y/8, answer 5xy/7. p19-q2-b: 8/5 ÷ (2y/3), answer 12/(5y), y ≠ 0; p19-q2-d: 6a/7 ÷ (2/5), answer 15a/7. p20-q3-b: (4x/5) ÷ 4, answer x/5; also change its comparison partner p20-q3-a to 4 × (4x/5), answer 16x/5, preserving the common expression and multiplier. p20-q3-c: 3 ÷ (x/5), answer 15/x, x ≠ 0. Retain the existing instructions.

findings.doneWhen: Every unnecessary later copy has different values and correct answers, while the multiplication/division contrast in p20-q3-a and p20-q3-b is preserved.

findings.finding: The opening review does not rehearse multiplying two algebraic terms, although the examples require both different-pronumeral and repeated-pronumeral products.
findings.breakdown: Every multiplication item in p12-q1 can be completed by numerical scaling alone. Students must then combine 2a × 3b and 4x × 3x, including recognising x × x as x², without rehearsing those substantial prior skills.
findings.checked: The earlier teaching and immediately preceding topic practise collecting terms and numerical scaling, not multiplying two variable-bearing terms. p12-q2 and p12-q3 rehearse numerical fractions; p12-q4 rehearses cancellation. The topic's multiplication rule does not explain how the algebraic numerator products simplify.
findings.assumptions: Multiplication of algebraic terms is prior knowledge from introductory algebra and indices. This finding concerns recall; it does not depend on calculator access.

repair.proposal: Append three short parts to p12-q1-root: g) 2a × 3b; h) 4x × 3x; i) 3a × 7a. Answers: 6ab; 12x²; 21a². Keep the complete opening review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The review rehearses products of different and repeated pronumerals before the worked examples use them.

findings.finding: In the supplied order, unscaffolded three-operand expressions precede the exercise's preparation for mixed multiplication and division.
findings.breakdown: After p20-q3's two-operand tasks, p21-q7 simultaneously introduces three operands, multiple variable cancellations and successive divisions. Students encounter the selective-inversion cue and three-factor working spaces only afterwards in p20-q4.
findings.checked: The examples and preceding division practice use two operands. Earlier numerical three-factor multiplication does not rehearse selective inversion or successive division. p20-q4 already supplies a bridge through three-factor mixed operations and progressively more involved variable cancellation. The harder label alone does not resolve this ordering problem.
findings.assumptions: The supplied block order governs student encounters, despite the page and question numbers. No calculator assumption is needed.

repair.proposal: Move p21-q7 to immediately after p20-q4.

findings.doneWhen: Students complete p20-q4's selective-inversion scaffold before attempting p21-q7.

findings.finding: Extend the existing final part with a sequence that holds the numerator calculation fixed while changing the common denominator.
findings.breakdown: This exposes how the common denominator affects the simplified result without changing the addition of like terms.
findings.checked: The proposed results are correct for every p. Existing guided practice varies denominators, but also changes coefficients, pronumerals or operations; it does not supply this controlled comparison.
findings.assumptions: Simplifying numerical factors is available from the review.

repair.proposal: After p5-q2-h, add one instruction: 'Predict which results will be whole algebraic terms before calculating.' Under the existing question instruction append i. 7p/8 + p/8 (answer p); j. 7p/4 + p/4 (answer 2p); k. 7p/2 + p/2 (answer 4p); l. 7p/16 + p/16 (answer p/2). Follow with the unpatterned part m. 5p/12 + 4p/12 (answer 3p/4). Across i–l, the numerator terms stay fixed and only the common denominator varies.

findings.doneWhen: The four-part comparison and unpatterned follow-up appear under p5-q2 with only the single prediction instruction added.

findings.finding: Extend Cedric's spending question by comparing the amount spent with the amount remaining.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects complementary amounts with addition and subtraction of algebraic fractions.
findings.checked: Rent and groceries total 7x/12; the remainder is 5x/12; their difference is x/6. Whole-term conversion and subtraction have been taught.

repair.proposal: Append d) Write a simplified algebraic fraction for the income Cedric has left after rent and groceries. Answer: 5x/12 dollars. e) How much more does he spend on rent and groceries than he has left? Answer: x/6 dollars.

findings.doneWhen: The two follow-up parts use Cedric's existing income and spending fractions.

findings.finding: Compare two sections whose different dimension multipliers produce the same area.
findings.breakdown: Students connect the product of the dimension multipliers with the fraction of the original area.
findings.checked: Both (x/2)(3y/4) and (3x/4)(y/2) equal 3xy/8. The original proposed third section would require breadth 3y/2, exceeding the field's breadth; replacing that part with a comparison preserves the intended relationship using multiplication already taught.
findings.assumptions: The field dimensions x and y are positive, and the sections lie within it.

repair.proposal: Append d) Another section has length 3x/4 and breadth y/2. What is its area? Answer: 3xy/8 m². e) Explain why this section has the same area as the section in part b. Expected answer: the dimension multipliers have the same product, since (3/4)(1/2) = (1/2)(3/4) = 3/8.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up compares two valid sections with equal areas using methods available by the end of the topic.

findings.finding: Contrast multiplication and division by a number and its reciprocal while keeping the initial algebraic fraction fixed.
findings.breakdown: The sequence exposes why dividing by 2 matches multiplying by 1/2, while dividing by 1/2 matches multiplying by 2.
findings.checked: All proposed answers are correct for every x or a. Between consecutive comparison parts, only the operation or the second operand changes. Existing practice does not provide this reciprocal comparison with a fixed initial fraction.
findings.assumptions: Fraction multiplication and division are available by the end of this topic.

repair.proposal: After p20-q3-f add one instruction: 'Predict which results will be equal before simplifying.' Append g. (x/5) × 2 (answer 2x/5); h. (x/5) ÷ 2 (answer x/10); i. (x/5) ÷ (1/2) (answer 2x/5); j. (x/5) × (1/2) (answer x/10). Follow with unpatterned part k. (3a/7) ÷ (2/5) (answer 15a/14).

findings.doneWhen: The comparison and unpatterned follow-up appear under p20-q3 with only the single prediction instruction added.

findings.finding: Connect division by a unit fraction with the matching multiplication calculation.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up makes the reciprocal relationship visible using the expression already in the exercise.
findings.checked: With the duplicate repair applied, part a becomes 4 × (4x/5) = 16x/5. Dividing 4x/5 by 1/4 gives the same result. The divisor is nonzero, and the calculation is valid for every real x.
findings.assumptions: The accompanying duplicate repair to p20-q3-a is applied.

repair.proposal: Append g) Simplify (4x/5) ÷ (1/4). Answer: 16x/5. h) Explain why your answer to part g equals your answer to part a. Expected answer: dividing by 1/4 is multiplying by its reciprocal, 4.

findings.doneWhen: The extension uses the same expression and matching reciprocal as the revised multiplication item.

protectedGroups.observation: The same numerator addition applies whether the common denominator is 1 or 4.
protectedGroups.invariant: The numerators x and 2x, and the addition operation.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing both side lengths changes area by the square of the side multiplier; halving sides and halving area require different operations.
protectedGroups.varies: The side multiplier, its representation and whether the side change or area change is given.
protectedGroups.invariant: The original square has side x and area x².

protectedGroups.observation: Successive reductions multiply the side factor repeatedly and square the resulting factor for area.
protectedGroups.varies: One reduction, two reductions and n reductions.
protectedGroups.invariant: The side reduction factor is 3/5 and the original area is x².

protectedGroups.observation: Adding and subtracting the same fractional multiple changes only the numerator calculation.
The denominator conversion stays the same when the operation changes.
Subtracting a smaller unit fraction from 2pi leaves a larger result.
protectedGroups.varies: The denominator of the subtracted fraction: 3, 4, 6.
protectedGroups.invariant: Starting amount 2pi, subtraction, and numerator pi.
